If it is the Ukthya sacrifice, then the Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra hymn comes first; however, it is indeed the Agniṣṭoma [that is the norm]. This has already been explained. All the stotras consist of seventeen verses.
Thus ends the second Svarasāman. 3.

The third [stotra] of the Svarasāmans is the third Svarasāman: "With flashing luster, these drops have been poured forth; the King goes with the songs of wisdom. Flow for us, O Pavamāna, like rain—of you, the wise one... (RV IX.59.2–3). Thus ends the Bahiṣpavamāna.
Flow on, O bull, for the sake of the five cups. (1) "By fire is fire kindled. These are the *ājya* verses. (2)

"High is the birth of your pressed juice"—this is the Gāyatra and the Cāmahīyava; "Toward us, O Soma, the Āyus"—this is the Paurumadga and the Gautama; and the Antarikṣa and the Agne-triṇidhana. "The three voices"—this is the final Saṃkrośa of the Aṅgirases. || 3 ||
[Thus concludes the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
The Paurumadga [Sāman] is on the first [verse]; the Agni-triṇidhana [Sāman] is on the middle [verse]. 3.
"pratyasmai pipīṣate" is the Rathantara; "vayaṃ gha tvā sutāvantaḥ" is the Vāmadevya; and "abhīvarta" is the Kāleya—all performed on their own respective verses.
Thus end the *pṛṣṭhas*.
In the Rathantara [sāman], there are two Anuṣṭubhs at the beginning; the last is a Bṛhatī.
In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, there are the Svarasāman chants. [The first three days consist of:

the Gāyatra, the Saṃhitā, and the Kṣullakavaiṣṭambha, with the verse "tisro vāca udīrate" (Three voices arise). Then the Vācaḥsāman with the verses "ā sotā pariṣiñcata sakhāya ā niṣīdata" (O friends, pour out the pressed juice; sit down), and the Sujñāna, or the Daivodāsa. [The next three days consist of: the Gaurīvita on three verses; the Gaurīvita on one verse; the Āndhīgava on one verse; and the Tvāṣṭrīsāman on one verse—or alternatively, the Svara on three verses, using that which is first as the Pavitra, and the Ariṣṭa as the last.
If one should conceptualize the *svāra* as the king of melodies (*sāmarāja*). || 5 ||
[Thus ends the Ārbhava Pavamāna.

Regarding the phrase "yat prathamam" (that which is first), this refers to the verse beginning with "sutāsaḥ madhumattamāḥ" (the pressed juices, most rich in sweetness). One should optionally employ the *svāra-sāman* as the *rājana*. This is to be explained as before. || 5 ||
The *yajñāyajñīya* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.

The *pramahiṣṭhīya*, the *hārivarṇa*, and the *udvaṃśīya* are the *uktha* chants; however, if it is an *agniṣṭoma* rather than an *ukthya*, [these apply]. The arrangement for the two *saṃsthās* is as before.
All [the days] consist of seventeen [stomas]. || 8 ||

All the *svarasāman*s are seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*). The word "all" signifies totality; the meaning is that all the *stotra*s for others are seventeen-fold. Alternatively, even though they are prescribed elsewhere by the author of the ritual manual (*kalpakāra*), the *svāra* verses are recited in their modified form (*ūha*). For example, "yaj jāyayā" is the *payonidhana*; "matsya pāyi te maha" is the *bṛhannidhana*; and "pratyasmā" is the first [of these]. Their application is among the *svarapṛṣṭha*s, which are *svarasāman*s. As it has been stated: "If they are *svarapṛṣṭha*s, then in the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* belonging to the *svarasāman*s, they are used according to the original text," and so forth. (8)
Thus end the Svarasāmans. 4.
On the day called Viṣuvat, some perform the Prātaranuvāka for the Viṣuvat; others chant the Bahiṣpavamāna outside [the sacrificial ground]. Thus he speaks of the day known as Viṣuvat, the Divākīrtya:
"Sing forth, O men, to the tawny one who has been pressed; like chariots that have been urged on, so are your songs for you, O Sage, as you flow clear. (RV 9.11.1)
Thus ends the Bahiṣpavamāna.
May Agni strike down the Vṛtras, when today at the rising of the sun, he has indeed risen up toward the famous wealth; this [is the prayer] from my mind for you two. 2.
Thus end the offerings of clarified butter.

The *Gavāmayana* sacrifice has the *Viṣuvant* day; following its ancient splendor are the *Gāyatram*, the *Bhrājam*, and the *Satrāsāhīyam*. "O Soma, with thee I have rejoiced"—this is the *Utsedha* in three verses; the *Ābhīśavam* in one verse, the *Abhīvarta* in one verse, and the *Pṛśni* in one verse; the *Rathantaram* in three verses; and the *Pārtha* hymn beginning with "To the infant newly born" is the final one. || 3 ||
[Thus ends the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
The Sāman-ṛcas beginning with the Ābhīśava; in the Śukriya hymns beginning with the Bhrāja, they should chant the *stobhas* three times; there is no repetition of what precedes the *nidhana*. 3.
The Mahādivākīrtya and the Vāmadevya; the Vikarṇa with "Indrakratuṃ na ā bhara"; and the Kāleya upon its own verses.
Thus end the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].

"Let the Mahādivākīrtya drink"—this is the specific rule for the *pṛṣṭha* oblation. Indra is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this Mahādivākīrtya, or alternatively Sūrya; the metre (*chandaḥ*) is Jagatī; the deity (*devatā*) is Sūrya. The manner of its praise has already been stated in the explanation of the *pratihāra*. Regarding the first *prastāva*, there is the laying down of *kuśa* grass and the taking up of the *udgītha* with the syllable *oṃ*; this is not done in the second. Having praised with this, they should first consume the *atigrāhya* cups belonging to the *triṣṭubh* metre from the *camasa*s.
They should consume these *atigrāhya*s after praising with the *pṛṣṭha* chant during either of the two three-day periods, as well as on the *viṣuvat* day and the *viṣuvat*-like days.
With the *triṣṭubh* metre; because of the statement, "First [of all] from the cups," the consumption of the *nārāśaṃsa* cup is as previously described. || 4 ||

"Pari svāno giriṣṭhā" consists of the Gāyatra and the Abhrāja. "Abhi dyumnaṃ bṛhadyaśaḥ prāṇā śiśurmahīnām" consists of the Śapha and the Śrudhya; these two are single-verse hymns. "Paryūṣu" is the Śyāvāśva, consisting of one verse. "Purojitī vo andhasaḥ" is the Bṛhat, consisting of three verses. The Gaurīvita is in one verse; the Āndhīgava is in one verse; the Niṣedha is in one verse; and the Yajñāyajñīya is in three verses. "Dhartā divaḥ" is the Kārya, which is the final [hymn]. 5.
[Thus ends the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
"paryū ṣu" is an Anuṣṭubh verse with a pipīlikā-madhyā (antepenultimate) cadence. 5.
"O head of heaven, messenger of earth"—this is the *bhāsa* chant with ten *stobhas*, the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
The twenty-one-fold hymn-form. || 7 ||

The *triṣṭubh* is its metre. Regarding the arrangement of the *stomas* for this day, it says, "the twenty-one-fold *stoma*. The *stotrīya* verses—"baṇ mahām̐ asi sūrya," "indram id devatātaye," and "śrāyanta iva sūryam"—are subject to option. Some transpose [these] in the *yajñāyajñīya* and *bhāsa* [sāmans]. The application of "tavāham" is to the *mahādivākīrtya*, and that of "purojitī" is to the *vikarṇa*, both in the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha* [rite]. As it has been stated: "If it is the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*, then the *pratipad* begins with 'agriyavatī'," and so forth.
Regarding the recitation in this section of "śrāyanta" from the *Vikarṇa* and "uccā te" from the *Agnivratas*, its purpose must be investigated.
Thus ends the equinox. 5.

The Svarasāmans are reversed; thus, on the subsequent wing, three Svarasāmans are reversed. These same reversed Abhiplavas follow after the Viṣuvat day. Regarding them, one should proceed in reverse order for the days of the Pṛṣṭhas and Svarasāmans, according to the scriptural injunction. He states their specific details: "O Indra, bring us wisdom"—this is the Mahāvaiṣṭambha; the Śyaita and Naudhasa are the Brahmasāmans of the reversed Svarasāmans in the Abhīvarta world. The Pauṣkala is for the two Rāthaṃtaras; the Śrudhya is for the Bārhata in the Sujñāna world.

Since it is heard in the scripture that "whatever *pragātha* occurs previously [is followed by] a different *sāman*," various *brahmasāmans* have been prescribed in place of the *abhīvarta* within the *indrakratu*. Although well-known, this [rule] pertains only to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, in its place, the *pauṣkala* is prescribed for the two *svarasāmans* belonging to the *rathantara*, and the *śrudhya* is prescribed for the *svarasāman* belonging to the *bṛhat*. Among those repeated *svarasāmans*, the first begins with "davidyutatyā ruce" and so forth; its [deity is] Indra.

In the *kratu* sacrifice, the *Brahmasāman* is the *Mahāvaiṣṭambha*. In the world of *Sujñāna*, it is the *Pauṣkala*. The second [sacrifice], however, has the *Svarasāman*; its *Brahmasāman* is the *Śyaita*, beginning with "pavasva vāco agriyaḥ. In place of the *Sujñāna* [verse] "indram accha," there is the *Śrudhya*. In place of the former of the two *Bṛhannidhana* tones, the latter [is used]. The third [sacrifice], however, begins with "upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ. Its *Brahmasāman* is the *Naudhasa* for the *Indrakratu*. In place of the *Sujñāna* [verse] "pavate haryato hariḥ," there is the *Pauṣkala*. The remainder is as before. || 1 ||
Thus end the Svarasāmans in their recurring order. || 6 ||
The Viśvajit; now he recites the Viśvajit:

"Toward you, O singer, the songs of kinship go forth like women seeking their husbands; and may that which is most desirable of Savitṛ be ours among our dear things. "O Agni, come hither; flow clear for Soma, the one who makes the sound. "Of you, O Sage, who are being purified... || 1 ||
Thus ends the Bahiṣpavamāna.

The first six [verses] consist of single *ṛc*s; the last is a triplet (*tṛca*), according to the Śruti statement, "The last is a triplet," and because of the rule that "the final [verse] is always a triplet when a *stoma* is possible. The *bahiṣpavamāna* has various deities. Agni, Sarasvatī, Sarasvant, Savitṛ, Brahmaṇaspati, and Pavamāna Agni are the deities of the six verses in their respective order. The subsequent triplet belongs to Pavamāna. 1.

The Gavāmayana and Viśvajit [are described] in Book 2, Section 7. "Well-kindled, bring [the gods] hither to us; may you be able for us regarding that which is earthly. They yoke the ruddy, glowing [horse]; praise him who [shines] with his flame.
(2) Thus the Ājya [stotras] are established in the four-verse hymn according to the lineage; the method of extraction has been stated. (2)

For this [Stotra], there are the Gāyatra and the Āmahīyava [Sāmans] set to the verse *asya pratnāmanu dyutam*. The Kāleya is on one verse with the words *parītoṣiñcatā sutam*; the Rathantara on three verses; the Dairghaśravasa on three verses; and the Yaudhājaya on one verse. The Pārtha is the final [Sāman] with the words *ayaṃ somaḥ*. [Thus ends the Mādhyandina Pavamāna. The Bṛhatī [verse] is composed with the ear of a hare. At the time of the Rathantara praise, the sound of a chariot must be made. One should perform the ritual rules (*dharmas*) for the Vairāja [Sāman] in the Viśvajit sacrifice, because of the statement: "According to the teacher's opinion, [these rules apply] even in other Pṛṣṭha [Stotras]. || 3 ||
The Vairāja, the Mahānāmnīs, the Vairūpa, and the Revatīs—these are the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. || 4 || Thus end the *pṛṣṭhas*.
"Let him drink the stainless, pleasant honey"—this is the *pṛṣṭha-homa*. The ritual rules for these *pṛṣṭhas* have been demonstrated in the section on the *pṛṣṭhya*.

"Pari svāno giriṣṭhāḥ" is the Gāyatra-saṃhitā; "pavasvendramaccha" is the Satrāsāhīya for the Śrudhya; "paryū ṣu" is the Vāmadevya; "purojitī vo andhasaḥ" is the Āndhīgava on one verse, the Gaurīvita on one verse, the Yadvāhiṣṭhīya on one verse, and the Yajñāyajñīya on three verses; "pari pra dhanve" is the Vāravantīya in the Dvipadās, and the Kāva ending with verses containing the word "sūrya. 5.
[Thus ends the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
"paryū ṣu" is an Anuṣṭubh with a Pipīlikamadhyā meter; "paripradhanva" is an Akṣarapaṅkti. || 5 ||
"O Agni, you are the Hotṛ of sacrifices"—this is the Bṛhat Agniṣṭoma Sāman.
Its meter is the Gāyatrī; at the time of praise, the sound of a drum should be made.
In the case of the Sarvastoma, the stomas are performed four times each, with three leadings forward.

Thus [it is said]. This should be explained according to the *Abhijit-stomakalpa*. Regarding this, the Śruti states: "They lead forward four *trivṛt* [stomas] for the Viśvajit; four *pañcadaśa*, and four *saptadaśa*. Thus, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is *trivṛt*; the *hotṛ*'s *ājya* is *pañcadaśa*; the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s is *saptadaśa*; and the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s is *ekaviṃśa*: such is the first leading forward (*praṇaya*). The *acchāvāka*'s is *pañcadaśa*; the midday *pavamāna* is *saptadaśa*.

The *pṛṣṭha* chant of the Hotṛ is the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*); that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is the twenty-seven-fold (*triṇava*)—this is the second [set]. That of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*); that of the Acchāvāka is the twenty-one-fold; the Ārbhava is the twenty-seven-fold; and the Agniṣṭoma is the thirty-three-fold (*trayastriṃśa*)—this is the third [set]. Thus, the *stomas* are repeated four times with three leadings (*triṣpraṇaya*). || 7 ||
Thus ends the Viśvajit sacrifice.
The Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods] are repeated; then follows the six-day Pṛṣṭhya period beginning with the thirty-three-fold stoma. He states the specific distinction for its six days:

The Gavāmayana consists of the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods], the Paurumīḍha, the Mānava, the Janitra, the Bhāradvāja, the Vāsiṣṭha, the Gauṅgava, and the Śuddhāśuddhīya; these are the single-verse hymns (ekarcas). For the revolving Pṛṣṭha [period], there is the Ābhīvarta Loka-stotra.

In that regard, first, for the *trayastriṃśa* day, [the stotra] begins with "pravājino na vājinaḥ" and so forth. For that [day], in place of the *abhīvarta*, there is the *paurumīḍha* [stotra] beginning with "pavamānābhyarṣasi. Regarding the sixth day, the six rules for the conclusion (*saṃsthā*) of the six-day period mentioned in the *Nidāna-sūtra*—beginning with "when the sixth day has concluded"—are to be performed on this day. How so? Because, having introduced the topic with "How are the concluding rules applied when the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are reversed?", the *Nidāna* states: "But for the *trayastriṃśa*, the teachers say [they apply] at the conclusion," and so forth.

The second twenty-seven-versed day begins with *pavamānasya viśvavit* and so forth; for this day, the *mānava* hymn is placed in the position of the *abhīvarta* with the verse *mandrayā yāti dhārayā*. The third twenty-one-versed day begins with *pavamāno ajījanat*, *punāno akramīd abhi*, and so forth; for this day, the *janitra* hymn is placed in the *abhīvarta* position with the verse *paridhim ratim*. The fourth seventeen-versed day begins with *davidyutatyā*; for this day, the *bharadvāja* hymn is placed in the first *abhīvarta* position with the verse *abhi somāsa āyavaḥ*.

The fifteenth day, beginning with *pavasva vāco agriyaḥ*, is the fifth [Agniṣṭoma]. In that [day], the Vāsiṣṭha hymn, beginning with *utso devo hiraṇyayaḥ*, takes the place of the Abhīvarta. The sixteenth day, beginning with *upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*, is the Trivṛt [Agniṣṭoma]. For that [day], the Gauṅgava or the Śuddhāśuddhīya hymn takes the place of the Abhīvarta in the first [stotra], beginning with *pra soma devavītaye*. Everything else is as before. || 1 ||

Now he states the specific details for the six days of the non-repeated *abhiplava* in their proper order: "O Indra, bring us wisdom" (*indra kratuṃ na ā bhara*) is the *paurumīḍha*; the *mānava*, *janitra*, *bhāradvāja*, *śyaita*, and *naudhasa* [are the other chants]. These are the *brahmasāmans* of the non-repeated *abhiplava* in the world of the *abhīvarta*. The *pauṣkala* is for the *rathantara*-verses and the *śrudhya* is for the *bṛhat*-verses in the world of *sujñāna*.

Thus [it is said]. Therein, the ritual procedure for the first day is as follows: "The prize-winners have been let loose," "This one, indeed, the ten fingers [have pressed]," and "O Sage, of thee, the purifying one," [constitute] the Bahiṣpavamāna, and so forth. "O Indra, bring us mental power" is the Paurumīḍha [Stotra] in place of the Abhīvarta Brahmasāman. "Him, O friends, of you... is the Śrudhya of Sujñāna.

For the second day: "Of the purifier, the all-knowing," and so forth; "O Indra, [grant] wisdom" is the *Brahmasāman* beginning with the *Mānava*; "The vital breaths are the child" is the *Pauṣkala* in the world of *Sujñāna*.

The *pavamāna* chant of the third day begins with "He has generated," and so forth. "O Indra, at the rite, the birthplace is the *brahmasāman*; Soma, being purified, is to be heard in the world of the wise."

On the fourth day: "With light that flashes like lightning," and so forth; the *Brahmasāman* is the *Indrakratu*, belonging to Bhāradvāja. "O friends, sit down together"—this is the *Pauṣkala*, [to be sung] in the world of Sujñāna.

For the fifth day, [the chant begins] with "Purify yourself, the foremost of speech," and so forth. At the *indrakratu* [stotra], the *śyaita* is the *brahmasāman*. At the place of the *sujñāna*, the *śrudhya* is used for the verse beginning with "Indra, come hither."
The *gavāmayana* is the life-span [of the sacrifice];

for the sixth day, [the chant begins] with "Sing to him, O men," and so forth. The *brahmasāman* is the *naudhasa*, beginning with "Indra’s deed. The *pauṣkala* is [chanted] on the verse "The beloved one flows" in the world of Sujñāna. Everything else has been stated. And here, when three *abhiplava* periods are to be performed, there is an omission of the first of the four repeated *abhiplavas*, which consists of the *śākvara* and *vaṇavān* [sāmans].

Regarding the northern *abhiplava* periods near the ten-night (*daśarātra*) cycle, Dhanañjaya maintains that among the three [sets] of four [days] that are repeated, the first should be omitted, so that the *iṣovṛdhīya* and the *samanta* would be at the end. This is the opposite view of Śāṇḍilyāyana. And regarding the vicinity of the *viṣuvat*: in this manner, there is an absence [of repetition] among the three [sets] on the subsequent side; thus, in the first month, there are twenty-eight days, and thirty-two in the last. However, two days will occur beforehand.

They should perform the *pṛṣṭhya* reversed and the *abhiplava* days in reverse order; that constitutes one month. In the same manner, there are three further months. Then, in the sixth month, there are three *abhiplavas* as before.
Thus end the repetitions of the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods].
He calls the Āyuṣṭoma the Āyuḥ;
the Jyotiṣṭoma the Ājyabahiṣpavamāna; and the Gāyatrī. 1.

By the word *gāyatrī*, the *gāyatra* triplet beginning with the *mādhyaṃdina* [stotra] together with its *sāman* is here denoted. The *bahiṣpavamāna* is "upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ. The *ājya* stotras are "agna ā yāhi," "mitrāvaruṇā," and "indrāgnī. The *gāyatra* and *cāmahīyava* are "uccā te jātam andhasaḥ. The [stotra] beginning with "abhi somāsa āyavaḥ" consists of two *hiṃkāras*, the *vārkajambha*, the *maidhātitha* which has the *bṛhat* as its *nidhana*, and either the *raurava* or the *yaudhājaya*; the *auśana* is the final one. 1–2.
Thus ends the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
There is a double *hiṃ* in the first [verse]; the *Yaudhājaya* [sāman] is in the middle verse. 2.
The Rathantara and the Vāmadevya; "O Indra, bring us mental power"—this is the Nodhas [Sāman], and the Kāleya among its own [verses]. 3.
Thus end the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].

"svādiṣṭhyā" is in the Gāyatra-Saṃhitā; "pavasvendraṃ accha" is in the Sapha-Pauṣkala; "purojitī vaḥ" is in the Gaurīvita-Andhīgava; the last [verse] is in the Kāva. 4. Thus ends the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
The Yajñāyajñīya is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. || 5 ||
The Pramahiṣṭhīya, the Hārivarṇa, and the Udvaṃśīya are the Ukthas.
The Gavamayana; the stomas are the Go and Āyuṣṭoma. || 7 ||

The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant has the *trivṛt* (nine-verse) stoma; the *ājya* chants have the *pañcadaśa* (fifteen-verse) stoma; the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) has the *saptadaśa* (seventeen-verse) stoma; the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) has the *ekaviṃśa* (twenty-one-verse) stoma. Thus the *stoma* is accompanied by *ukthas*. This is the *āyuḥ* [sacrifice]. The *goṣṭoma*:
"Flow on, the foremost of speech, with flashing luster! Flow on, O Indu, as the pressed bull! O Soma, you are a bull, you are brilliant—of you, the purifying sage. (1)
Thus ends the Bahiṣpavamāna.
We choose Agni as our messenger. || 2 ||
Thus end the clarified butter offerings.

The *gāyatra* and *cāmahīyava*, beginning with "Asya pratnām anu dyutam"; the *samanta* and *vārkajambha*, beginning with "Parīto siñcatā sutam"; the *dainrghaśravasa* ending in the *nidhana* "Yadi," or the *bārhaduktha*; the *yaudhājaya*; and the *pārtha* ending with "Ayaṃ soma" as the final [stotra]. (3)
[Thus ends the Mādhyandina Pavamāna. It is performed all around on the first [stotra], and the Yaudhājaya on the middle one. 3.
The *Bṛhat* and the *Vāmadevya*; the *Śyaita* with the verse "O Indra, bring us wisdom" (*indra kratuṃ na ā bhara*), and the *Kāleya* upon its own verses. || 4 ||
Thus end the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
"yaste mado vareṇyaḥ" is for Auksai; "pavasvendram accha" is for Śrudhya; "purojitī vo andhasaḥ" is for Gauriviti; and the final [laud] for Nandhīgava consists of verses containing the word "sūrya."
[Thus ends the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
The Yajñāyajñīya is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. 6.
The Sākamaśva, the Saubhara, and the Udvaṃśīya are the Ukthas.
The Goṣṭoma is the Stoma. || 8 ||

The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant consists of fifteen verses; the *ājya* chants consist of nine verses; the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) consists of seventeen verses; and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) consists of twenty-one verses. This is the *stoma* known as the *soktha*.

Now, the ten days of the twelve-day sacrifice—beginning with the *trivṛt* day and ending with the *avivākya* day—are to be performed like the expanded twelve-day sacrifice (*vyūḍha-dvādaśāha*) which has the character of a *sattra*.

Sing forth the great vow for him, O men; sing unto him who is born, the overcomer of waters. Flow on, O Indu, as the foremost of speech. Flow on, O Indu, as the bull, pressed out; he shines with flashing luster. These drops have been poured forth like grain after grain by our means, O Sage, as you flow clear. 1.
Thus ends the Bahiṣpavamāna.
The Gavāmayana and the Mahāvrata, Chapter 2, Section 11:
The immortal god, the Hotṛ—him who fashions beautiful forms, bestow him upon us for our protection. Pour out the beloved [Soma] into the pressed juice for our aid. 2.
Thus end the clarified butter offerings.

On this day, the *pañcaviṃśastoma* (twenty-five-verse hymn-form) belongs to all the *stotras*. Its *viṣṭuti* (method of chanting) is as follows: He utters the *hiṃ* call for eight verses—three times, four times, and once. He utters the *hiṃ* call for eight verses—once, three times, and four times. He utters the *hiṃ* call for nine verses—four times, twice, and [three times].

"He with three; he with five; he with one; he with three"—thus it is said. Gautama says that one should insert [these] in the final *paryāya* of the twenty-four-fold stoma during the *paricara*. Dhānaṃjayya says that this is the place for insertion. || 2 ||

Following its ancient luster: the *gāyatram*, the *cāmahīyavam*, the *jarābodhīyam*, and the *satrāsāhīyam*; "Pour out the pressed juice on every side": the *samantam*, the *dairghaśravasam*, and the *rauravayaudhājaye*; "This is the Soma": the *pārtham* as the final [stotra]. (3)

Thus ends the Mādhyandina Pavamāna. Regarding the Yaudhājaya [Sāman], it is to be performed on the Adhyāsyā verses; for there is a scriptural injunction stating, "One [verse] at the very end, on the Adhyāsyā itself. (3) The Vrata is the Pṛṣṭha. (4) This means that what is about to be described, designated as the Vrata, is the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha. (4)
There are thirteen types of intoxication ordained by Brahmā. || 5 ||

The meaning is that, by means of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "By the vital breath in front," thirteen chants designated as *parisāman* are prescribed as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the *pṛṣṭha* stotra. Their status as auxiliary parts of the *pṛṣṭha* is stated for the purpose of accomplishing the twenty-five-fold perfection (*pañcaviṃśa-sampat*) of the *pṛṣṭha*. Accordingly, the *Upagrantha* states: "The head, wings, and tail consist of three sets of twenty-five. For that very reason, although these are *parisāmans*, their performance (*gāna*) is prescribed in the Sūtra to be done only once.

"Indramid gāthino bṛhat," "Indro dadhīco asthabhir," and "Udghed abhi śrutāmagham"—this *trivṛt* is the head, in the *gāyatra* metre. The *pañcadaśa* *rathantara* is the right wing; the *saptadaśa* *bṛhat* is the left wing; the *ekaviṃśa* *bhadra* is the tail. "Tad id āsa bhuvaneṣu jyeṣṭham"—this *pañcaviṃśa* is the body, the *rājana* chant. (6) Thus the *pṛṣṭha* known as the *vratas* has been described. At the *pṛṣṭha-homa*, the specific difference is that the *mahāvrata* chant is used with the verse beginning "pibatu somyam."

Because of the statement "the great vows" (*mahāvrata*) and the word "vow" (*vrata*), [one should recite] either "May the *Gāyatra*, *Rathantara*, *Bṛhat*, and *Rājan* [Sāmans] drink the Soma-mead, bestowing long life upon the lord of the sacrifice," or one should recite all those which constitute the *pṛṣṭha* [laud] stotras. This is because of the rule that one should modify the words "drink" and "bestowing" according to the context. However, the former view is that of Gautama:

they should mutter the three triplets beginning with "Indramid gāthinaḥ," the three triplets for the *Rathantara*, *Bṛhat*, and *Bhadra* [Sāmans], and the triplet beginning with "Tadidāsa" right there in the *sadasya* [hall]. Alternatively, they may mutter them at the very place where each respective *stotra* is performed.

The Gavāmayana and the Mahāvrata are the primary locations for the ancillary rites (*aṅga*). However, following the recitation of the *ṛc*, one should perform the recitation of the ten *vyāhṛtis* as appropriate and the recitation of "That which is in the cows" (*yaste goṣu*), according to the statement in the *Upagrantha*: "Indeed, the *gāyatra* [sāman] departs from the *vratas* upon the recitation of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*. Now, Bhāḍitāyana maintains that once the *pṛṣṭha* has been introduced, having yoked the *stoma*, one should sing the *parimada*. Gautama and Śāṇḍilya, as well as Dhānañjayya, maintain that after performing the *ṛc*-recitation and receiving the response, one should yoke the two blades of grass.

Some say that one should perform the recitation of the *ṛc* verses even before the preparation for the hymn of praise (*stotra*). Having exited by the eastern door and gone to the south of the *Āgnīdhrīya* shed and to the north of the great fire-altar (*mahāgnicayana*), they should worship with the [verses] beginning with "Prāṇa. The Udgātṛ should chant all the *sāmans* once each. The Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ should follow the finale (*nidhana*) [of the chant]. Even in the case of *sāmans* that have a middle finale, they should follow the middle finales. In those [sāmans] that are bound at the beginning and end and possess terminal syllables (*pāra*), they should insert the musical interjections (*stobha*) after every word.

Standing to the east of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) facing west, they should worship the *Āhavanīya* fire with the *Sāman* based on the out-breath (*prāṇa*). Its seers are Vasiṣṭha, Triṣṭubh, and Indra. Having uttered "hāu hāu hāu" and taken a breath, one should recite the *stobhas* beginning with "āyuḥ satyam," step by step. Returning by that same path and standing behind the tail, they should worship the tail with the *Sāman* based on the in-breath (*apāna*). [Its seers are] Vasiṣṭha, Triṣṭubh, and Indra.

Having made a breath-hold with "hāu hāu hāu," one should chant the stobhas for each word beginning with "ā no āyāhi. [The sequence is: "hāu 3," "hiṃ hiṃ hiṃ," "ihā," and "hiṃ" according to the preceding rule for the two fortnights of the vow.

They should worship the right wing with the *sāman*; the left [wing] with the subsequent *sāman*. Prajāpati, the *triṣṭubh* meter, and Indra [are the deities]. One should chant the *stobha* for each step. Facing eastward, they should worship the chest of Prajāpati with the "Heart" hymn (*hṛdaya*). It is stated that the two wings and the two flanks are to be worshipped from behind. Its seer is Prajāpati, and he is also the deity. There is no meter. The phrase "ehṛdayām" is recited three times as the internal *nidhana*. "Prajārūpam," etc., is the *nidhana*.

With the verse "All the gods" (*viśve devāḥ*), which belongs to Vasiṣṭha, they should worship the *cātvāla* pit. Vasiṣṭha is the seer, the *jagatī* is the metre, and the Viśvedevas are the deities; [the priest] should chant the *stobha* for each successive word, beginning with "Come hither" (*ā ihi*). Having worshipped the *cātvāla*, they go to the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed and stand behind it facing east. While remaining in the position of the *cātvāla*, they then worship the *āgnīdhrīya* facing west, desiring success in the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Its seers are the sages and its deities are the Viśvedevas.

From each of the deity-words beginning with *aganma jyotiḥ*, one should chant the stobha *au hovā*. This is because they proceed like words [of a mantra]. [The verses are: "We have gone to the light; we have become immortal; we have ascended from the earth to the intermediate space; we have ascended from the intermediate space to heaven; we have found the gods; we have come together with the gods; the light of heaven! The *nidhanas* (concluding syllables) are as follows: for these [verses], they should pronounce the final *nidhana* as long as the breath lasts.

With the *sāman* verse "Hāu! Brahmāṇaḥ, invoke Indra," they should worship the *havirdhāna* shed from the east, facing west. And with the *anuśloka* verse "Hāu! Invoke [him] toward [us]," they should worship from the west, facing east. Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of these two; the metre is *triṣṭubh* beginning with two feet; Indra is the deity. Then, looking in that same direction, they should worship the *mārjālīya* shed with the *yāma* verse "Auhoi! The eagle in the firmament," which is studied among the *dvandva* hymns. Yama is the seer; the metre is *triṣṭubh*.

The Suparṇas, Varuṇa, and Yama are the deities. They should worship with the *āyuḥ* [verse] and the *navastobha* [verses] using the former *sāman*, standing to the east facing westward. With the latter [sāman], they perform the *gavāmayana* and the *mahāvrata* from behind.

They should stand facing east, chanting "hāu-hāu-hāu-vā. In the *āyuḥ* and *navastobha* [stotras], [the verses] are "viśvato dāvan" and so forth; Prajāpati is the *dvipadā viṣṭārapaṅkti*, and Indra is [the deity]. The *nidhanas* for these two have been stated. Standing within the altar (antarvedi) facing west, they should worship the Gārhapatya fire with the *ṛśya* Sāman; or rather, standing behind it facing east. The Gārhapatya is the same as the Śālāmukhīya. For the *ṛśya* Sāman, "harī ta indre," Kaśyapa is the seer, the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter, and Indra is the deity.

The *nidhana* is "ṛṣyāsa indra," and so forth. Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "They should employ the *nidhana* directly, beginning with Indra. This means that they should address him by saying, "O Indra, [thou who art] purified by the *tasara*. As for the *Nidāna*, it says: "That which is short is direct (*pratyakṣa*), while that which is lengthened is indirect (*parokṣa*)," and so on. Having performed the *parimad* chants in this manner, they should equip the King. Apart from the donning of armor, the Udgātṛ should cause the binding of the sword, bow, and other such items.

Two chariots, each with two excellent horses, should follow that king. Others than the king should prepare the sacrificial ground (devayajana) from the east. The king and his ministers should circumambulate the sacrificial ground by the south. The Udgātṛ, having gone to the wife’s hall (patnīśālā) by the east, should spread eastward-pointed Darbha grass at the southern edge of the altar and seat him there facing east. Then he should fasten the armor upon him, using the verse beginning "Arise, O King" and ending with "O protector," or he fastens it on another [person].

One should address the King with this mantra. Then, having been told by the attendants, "Go around by the west," the Udgātṛ, together with the King and his ministers, should proceed clockwise around the western side of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). The Udgātṛ, having turned back toward the wife’s hall (*patnīśālā*) by the eastern side and having stationed the King to the east of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire at the northern edge of the altar, should say: "The hand-guard," and so forth, ending with "the fourth. Its meaning is as follows: "Bind the leather hand-guard upon your hand; make the bow with its string drawn up."

"Prepare three arrows made of iron; for the fourth arrow, prepare any one at random without restriction. He should say, "Fit the two shafts to the bow. While the king is fitting them, he should address him with the mantra beginning with "O Vaiṇāvata" and ending with "hold fast. He should also say, "Stand firm with power. And the king, without handing over the shaft of the bow, should mount a chariot that is among those following him.

The sacrificer’s attendants should fasten two skins, one to the east and one to the west, to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire, leaving a path for the chariot to the south. Then the Udgātṛ should say to the King (Soma): "One should go around the sacrificial ground (devayajana) keeping it to the right," and so on, ending with "they should inspire confidence. The meaning of this is: while going around the sacrificial ground keeping it to the right, he should pierce the skins at the points where the front of the skin is reached.

"How shall they shoot, one after another, with iron arrows—placing the second upon the first, and the third upon that, without missing and without over-shooting—so as to easily pierce the other skin target? Having pierced with the third arrow, you should proceed northward together with your companions. Likewise, you should cast the fourth arrow in whichever direction you deem fit, saying, 'Slay the haters of Brahman! Upon seeing a cow, you should stop."

In that case, [thinking] "he may have gone somewhere and they might put on their armor," one should then direct another Brāhmaṇa to circumambulate the sacrificial ground (devayajana) from left to right, and so forth; this is the meaning of the *praiṣa* (directive). At the time of the *hiṃkāra*, having said, "Make this king [the Soma] proceed," the *udgātṛ* should go toward the earth-drum (*bhūmidundubhi*). Behind the *āgnīdhrīya* shed is the pit for the *gavāmayana* and the *mahāvrata*.

The drum-shaped [pit] is dug such that half is within the sacrificial altar (vedī) and half is outside the altar. It should be covered with the hide of a bull, with the hair facing upwards. The Udgātṛs should strike it with a leather thong while reciting the three mantras beginning with "tvaṃ vāgasi," one mantra for each stroke. Or, they should consecrate another person who is striking it by reciting these same mantras.

In the *aikāhika* and *āhīnika* vows, in the mantra beginning with "thou art speech," the word *yajña* (sacrifice) should be used in place of the word *satra* (session). Having consecrated the water with the formula "may they rejoice in the sacrifice" (*yajñe 'nandiṣuḥ*), and having touched it, they should turn back toward him and, standing behind, worship the piled fire-altar (*cityam agnim*) with the formula beginning "homage to thee, O Gāyatrī. This constitutes the head.

They should perform the worship (upasthāna) with the formula "Salutation to you, O Rathantara," for the right wing; with the formula beginning "Salutation to you, O Yajñāyajñīya," for the tail; and with the formula beginning "Salutation to you, O Vāmadevya," for the middle. Since, according to another alternative in the Brāhmaṇa, the Yajñāyajñīya is prescribed as the tail and the Vāmadevya as the body, the worship of the tail and the middle is performed with those two mantras based on their respective indicative marks (liṅga).

The author of the Sūtra has stated: "When [the sun is] in Bhadrarāja, they should worship the tail with 'Salutation to thee, O Bhadrāya,' the middle with 'Salutation to thee, O Rājanāya,' and [the rest]. Then, having worshipped the entire Agni with the complete mantra beginning with 'Salutation to thee, O Gāyatra' and ending with 'to that one... place [it],' they should enter the *sadas*."

Regarding this, when it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa, "There, all [the priests], together with the *ṛtvij*s, should praise with the *mahāvrata*," then, according to the alternative of praising after having performed the ritual distribution (*vihṛtya*), there is entry into the *sadas* immediately after the *agnyupasthāna*. For in that alternative, the praise is performed with the head and all other parts while remaining in the *sadas* itself. However, according to the alternative where "the *udgātṛ* alone should chant with the whole [body]," they should enter the *sadas* by the sequence beginning with "having praised with the head in the *havirdhāna*. In that case, the application is as follows: the arrangement of the *kuśa* grasses is distinct for the head, the wings, and the tail.

The *kuśa* grass, the implements, and the garments are each separate. Having performed the attendance upon the fire (*agnyupasthāna*), having entered the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, one places [the vessel] to the north of the Soma vessels in the middle of the *havirdhāna*, with the verse: "Indra, the singer of the lofty song; Indra with the bones of Dadhyañc; he who has lifted up the famous wealth."

They should praise with the *gāyatra* [sāman], which is unexpressed (*anirukta*), accompanied by the threefold hymn-form (*trivṛt-stoma*). In the four-verse hymn beginning with "Indramid gāthinaḥ," there is an extraction (*uddhāra*) of the final verse. The arrangement of the *kuśā* grass is performed according to the *viṣṭuti* known as the *saṃdhiṣāmavat-parivartinī*. The Śruti describes the form of a bird for the *gāyatra* and the others, using designations such as "head" and so forth. For the *gāyatra* designated as the "head," the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are Puṣkala, Gāyatrī, and Indra. There is the recitation for the sacrificer (*yajamāna-vācana*). And when the praise is completed by the *rājana* [sāman], the *acchidra-japas* (flawless mutterings) should be performed by all together in a common ritual procedure (*tantra*).

But it is not immediately after each respective praise. Thus, having praised the *havirdhāna* shed with their heads, they go back in haste by the western door. Having gone around the south of the *mārjālīya* hearth, and sitting behind the *maitrāvaruṇa* hearth, they should chant the *rathantara* in the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) stoma. After chanting, there is the bestowing of boons.

And so says the Upagrantha: "In the case of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* alone, one should indeed obtain the ritual duties (*dharma*) of the *vrata*. They should creep northward behind the *hotṛ*'s hearth; having sat down behind the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s hearth, they should chant the *bṛhat* with the seventeen-fold hymn."

They should emerge again by the same way they crept forward, exit through the eastern door of the *havirdhāna*, go around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed, and sit behind the *gārhapatya* fire; there they should chant the *puccha-stotra* with the twenty-one-fold hymn, according to the rule: "The auspicious twenty-one-fold is the tail. This is the chanting with the auspicious hymn. They should creep back by the same way they emerged, go around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya*, enter through the eastern door of the *havirdhāna*, and proceed westward while holding hands.
Having gone around the south of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths...

Having performed the Gavāmayana, the great rite, they should go to the *dhiṣṇya* hearth of the Maitrāvaruṇa and sit down by the way they came. Then, by the western door, they should enter the assembly hall (*sadas*) by means of a throne made of *udumbara* wood, which has been previously bound with a cord of *muñja* grass.

The attendants of the sacrificer [should act as follows]: in the absence of *udumbara* wood, a stool (*āsandī*) should be made from a sacrificial tree other than the *palāśa*. In the absence of *muñja* grass, the binding should be done with a cord of *darbha* grass. The legs of the stool should be one span (*prādeśa*) long; the other parts should be one cubit (*aratni*) long. Having carried such a stool to the south of the *audumbarī* post, they should place it to its north.

The Udgātṛ, having gone to the north of her and sat down behind her, should touch her while keeping her feet touching the ground and placing two bundles of *kūrca* grass beneath them: "The *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] are your two front feet"—thus the two front feet; "the *Śyaita* and *Naudhasa* [Sāmans] are the two hind ones"—thus the two hind feet; "the *Vairūpa* and *Vairāja* [Sāmans] are the two longitudinal ones"—thus the two side-boards facing east; "the *Śākvara* and *Raivata* [Sāmans] are the two transverse ones"—thus the two side-boards facing north. Having thus touched the individual parts, he performs the weaving, which is the binding with cords of *muñja* grass.

Having touched [the throne], he should recite the Ṛgvedic verses beginning with *prāñca ā tā na* and ending with the *yajñāyajñīya*. Therein, the touching of the various parts should be performed according to their respective characteristics. Having touched that throne with his face, chest, and arms, he should ascend it. The ascent is performed with the four mantras beginning with *vasavas tvā* and ending with *sāmrājyāya*. Having ascended, he should recite: "Sit upon the pleasant one; sit upon the comfort-giving one; homage be to thee; do not harm me."

When the Udgātṛ has thus ascended, the Prastotṛ, the Pratihartṛ, the Brahman, and the Gṛhapati shall also ascend their seats (*kūrca*) in the *ahīna* sacrifice; in a *sattra*, however, all [the priests] should ascend. The material for the seat (*āsandi*) has already been explained; it is made of *vāṇa*. By the word *vāṇa*, a specific type of lute is meant. It should be made of *udumbara* wood or from a sacrificial tree. Of that—

At the lower part of the staff, there is a circular cavity that is thicker than the dimensions of the staff and curved in shape. That region is covered with the hide of a red bull, with the hair facing upward. On its upper part, there are ten holes; in these, ten strings—either made of muñja grass or of bark—are tied one above the other. Alternatively, a hundred strings may be tied within the midst of all ten holes. How so?

There are thirty-four [strings] in the middle; thirty-three on each side. At their front, however, a binding should be made one by one. Having divided those [strings] into three parts, one should transfer them upward with each of the *vyāhṛtis*: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. With *bhūḥ*, one should transfer thirty-three; with *bhuvaḥ*, one should transfer thirty-four; and with *svaḥ*, one should transfer thirty-three. This transferring (*udūhana*) should be performed in both sections as well. One should touch that bow (*vāṇa*) with the mantra ending in "O bow (*vāṇa*), speak, speak! (*vado vada vāṇa*).

He should pull tight the loose threads with the mantra ending in *ebhir no vāṇā aśīmahi*. Having murmured *vāk sarvaṃ mano jyotir mano bhadram*, he should strike the arrow at its base with Indra’s *iṣīkā* (reed) and a branch of the *vetasa* tree together with its leaves. That which is naturally curved is "Indra’s *iṣīkā*. With *prāṇāya tvā*, he should scratch upwards; with *apānāya tvā*, he should scratch downwards; and with *vyānāya tvā vyānāya tvā*, having scratched three times, he should thrust the arrow towards the north.

Having addressed the Brahmin with the words, "Let him draw this arrow and let it fly," he should say, "Let the drums resound; let the lutes [resound]. At the eastern door, outside the *sadas*, they should cause the players of lutes—namely, those playing the gourd-lute (*alābu-vīṇā*), the curved lute (*vakrā*), and the *kapiśīrṇī*—to play.

The *gavāmayana* and the *mahāvrata* [are to be performed]. The *alābu-vīṇā* (gourd lute) is well known. A curved lute with a single string is called a *vetra-vīṇā*. A *kapiśīrṣṇī* is one with a monkey-head [top]. One should consecrate the two curved lutes (*vakrā*) and the *kapiśīrṣṇī*, as well as the drums (*dundubhi*), by reciting the mantra beginning with "He who [is] in the curved [lute]" and ending with "thus. Furthermore, the *mahāvīṇā* and the *piśīla-vīṇā* should be played either inside or outside at the western door. The *alābu-vīṇā* and the *mahāvīṇā* have fourteen strings. The *śūrpa-vīṇā* and the *piśīla-vīṇā* have black strings or golden strings.

And they should converse with one another, beginning with "Though without gain, he is virtuous," and ending with "He will be honored. To the west, the wives of the *udgātṛ*s should play two lutes each—one a *kāṇḍavīṇā* and the other a *picchoravīṇā*—alternating them. A *kāṇḍavīṇā* is made of reeds.

The *picchorā* is made of bamboo or of peacock feathers, or of reeds (*kāṇḍa*). By means of this instrument, one should play the *picchorā* near the mouth [of the drum]. These two are known by the name *apaghāṭilā*. One should consecrate them with mantras. While looking at everything, the wife should mutter [the mantra] beginning with "The *apaghāṭilā* which... and ending with "...the skin. [She should also mutter] "The cries, the *ulūlayas*... and ending with "...is sung. Then the *udgātṛ* priest should mutter [the mantra] beginning with "You are the *suparṇa* bird" and ending with "...the sacrificers."

In a sacrifice with a single patron (*ekayajamānaka*), when one desires heaven for this patron, the modification (*ūha*) should be made as follows: "This patron... A Brāhmaṇa should sit at the eastern door of the *sadas* facing west; he is called the *abhigara*. A Śūdra (vṛṣala) should sit at the western door facing east; he is the *apagara*. That Śūdra should say, "These performers of the sacrificial session (*sattrin*) have failed" (*nārātsuḥ*). The *abhigara* should say, "They have succeeded" (*arātsuḥ*). In a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) and a multi-day sacrifice (*ahīna*), the *apagara* should say, "This patron has failed" (*nārātsīd ayam yajamānaḥ*). The *abhigara* should say, "He has succeeded" (*arātsīt*).

To the south of the *mārjālīya* fire, a Vaiśya should stand within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) facing the south. To the outside of the altar, a Śūdra should stand facing the north; in the absence of a Vaiśya, any member of an Ārya caste may take his place. These two should compete for a white, circular hide. The Śūdra should compete first, and the Ārya afterwards. To the east of the *āgnīdhra* shed, a religious student (*brahmacārin*) should stand within the altar facing the north. To the outside of the altar, an unchaste woman, a woman of loose conduct, should stand facing the south.

She should say to the student, "I am a woman of ill-conduct, one who has broken her vow. And the student should reply to her, "Shame on you, you wretched woman! up to the words "O woman, [this is] the life-force of the penis. Again, the unchaste woman [speaks] as before; and the student [responds] as before. Again, the unchaste woman [speaks] as before.

The Gavāmayana, the Mahāvrata, and the Brahmachārī [are to be performed]. When all the rites, beginning with the *abhigara* and *apagara*, have been completed, the *abhigara* should say, "These performers of the sacrificial session (*sattrin*) have succeeded. However, if there is only a single sacrificer (*yajamāna*), he should say, "This sacrificer has succeeded. Then, having cast off the circular skin (*carma-maṇḍala*), a Śūdra should run away; a Vaiśya should strike him with that very skin. A loose woman (*puṃścalī*) may speak harshly to the Brahmachārī as she pleases. To the west of the *āgnīdhra* fire-shed, outside the altar and in an enclosed space, a couple should unite.

The two classes [of women] who would receive [the bride] are those born of marriage (*saṃbhava*) and those who are mistresses (*abhīṣṭā*). There should be at least five female slaves of the householder, or up to five hundred, or twenty-five. Having filled nine new jars with water, they should walk clockwise around the *mārjālīya* shed, saying, "Honey! This is honey! This is honey! They should also play lutes for them. Upon all the corners of the *sadas* hall, excluding the central one, they should tie up drums.

They should utter, as they obtain them, the words of the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, as well as worldly sounds such as those of musical instruments, each succeeding one after the other. Upon the *hiṃkāra* of the Rājanya, the *abhigara* and the others, having performed their respective duties, should depart. Having spoken the Brāhmaṇa passage, it is said that he should cause [the performance] to be done at the time of the *hiṃkāra*. At the time of the *hiṃkāra*, he should perform everything from the circumambulation of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) up to the looking toward the cows. Until the end of the *stotra*, the *kumbhinī* drums and all sounds such as the lute (*vīṇā*) continue.
Now follows the Rājanavrata. It has the Pañcaviṃśa-stoma; for it is stated that "the self is the Pañcaviṃśa, [and] the Rājanam. The Rājanam.

They know the twenty-fifth [verse] as Indra; it is a *triṣṭubh* verse, and Indra is its deity. The ritual applications (*bhakti*) have been stated. When the final *stotrīyā* verse has been introduced (*prastuta*), he should extend his feet. At the moment of the *nidhana*, he should place them on the ground. Having performed the recitation of the *ṛc* up to the end according to the command of the sacrificer, when the *bhakṣa* (soma) is being brought, he should descend with the *ārohaṇīya* mantras in reverse order: "May the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*) descend upon thee with the *anuṣṭubh* metre; following them, I descend for sovereignty"—this is the first mantra.

"May the Ādityas descend with the Jagatī metre; following them, I descend for self-sovereignty (*svārājya*)," is the second [formula]. "May the Rudras descend with the Triṣṭubh metre for sovereignty (*vairājya*)," is the third. "May the Vasus descend with the Gāyatrī metre for kingship (*rājya*)," is the fourth. Having descended with these four [formulas], he should mutter [the verse] beginning with "The great heaven... and ending with "...with nourishments. The consumption of the *atigrāhya* cups is performed first with the Triṣṭubh metre, prior to the *camasa* cups. Then follows the consumption of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups. || 6 ||
Regarding the others, he states the arrangement of the *stomas* for all [the days] except for the one designated as the *vrata-pṛṣṭha*: "The other is entirely twenty-five-fold."
Thus [ends the seventh].

The Vāmadevya, the Maitrāvaruṇa-sāman, [with the verse] "In the Trikadruka-sacrifices, the buffalo [drank] the barley-mash"—this Vāmadevya with five *nidhanas* is the Brahman-sāman; the Kāleya is [performed] on its own verses.
Thus end the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
Then, sitting down, they should praise with the Vāmadevya and other hymns; the Vāmadevya is in the Atichandas metre, and Indra is its deity. || 8 ||

The Gavāmayana, the Mahāvrata, and then the Ārbhava Pavamāna with the verses "parisvāno giriṣṭhā," the Gāyatra, the Svāśira, and the Marka; "pavasvendram accha" is the Sapha for Śrudhya; "purojitī vo andhasaḥ" is the Gaurīvita and the Madhuścunnidhana, and the Śyāvāśva and Andhīgava; in the verses containing "sūryavatīṣu," the Kāva is the final [stotra]. || 9 ||
[Thus ends the Ārbhava Pavamāna:

The Gaurīvita [is chanted] on a single verse; for there is the statement, "If it is the Ārbhava, then one [verse] is in the Anuṣṭubh meter," and also, "When making it consist of a single verse, one should place it at the beginning of the first [verse]. (9)
The Yajñāyajñīya is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. || 10 ||

Or it may be the *ilānda*. For there is a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) stating, "The *ilānda* should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*. Furthermore, there is the statement in the *Nidāna*: "The *sāmans* belonging to Satavaśva and Śyāvāśva are the *vrata* [sāman]. Agni is the established seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *viṣṭārapaṅkti* meter; "Agni" and so forth are the [other] details. The ritual portions (*bhaktis*), however, have already been explained. With the first *anugāna*, the spreading of *kuśa* grass is performed. In the case of the *ilānda*, the *yajñāyajñīya* should be performed in place of the *anuṣṭubh* [verse] belonging to Śyāvāśva.

Now, where there is another Agniṣṭoma-sāman, that [sāman] occurs in the Anuṣṭubh meter; this is the underlying principle (*nidāna*). At the end of the Agniṣṭoma, the rites beginning with the release of the *stoma* and ending with the *apsuṣoma* are performed. Here, in the Viśvajit, the Pṛṣṭhya-daśarātra, and the Mahāvrata, even though it is not being chanted, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin should recite the *indrakratu* hymn with the words "Bring us Indra’s power" (*indrakratuṃ na ābhara*). This is because of the rule stating that the *indrakratu* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin occurs everywhere after the Viṣuvat until the Atirātra. || 10 ||
Thus ends the Mahāvrata.

Now follows the *udayanīya* (concluding rite), specifically the *udayanīya-atirātra*. For that, the prosperity and other details of the entire *satra* apply everywhere. Regarding its performance, it is said: "The *udayanīya-atirātra* is established just as the *prāyaṇīya* [is]; it is just as the *prāyaṇīya*. When the rites beginning with the release of the *stomas* and ending with the consumption of curds have been performed for it, they should descend for the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath). This is stated: "When the *udayanīya-atirātra* has been completed, they should descend for the *avabhṛtha*. At the end of the *udavasānīya*, having chosen other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), they should perform sacrifices separately with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* offerings. The *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* has been described.
Thus ends the Udayanīya [offering]. 12.
Thus Varadarāja, the son of Ācārya Vāmana and born of the Kuśika lineage,
composed this commentary on the *Saṃvatsarakalpa* together with its practical application (*prayoga*).
Among those varieties of the Gavāmayana sacrifice that have been mentioned in the context of the Stomas,
some are described here for the purpose of making known the application of the modified Sāmans (ūha-sāman).
But those others which have not been shown here by us for fear of prolixity, they are to be found in the Sūtra itself; may the Supreme Person be pleased.
Thus ends the second chapter of this commentary on the Ārṣeyakalpasūtra, composed by Varadarāja, son of the venerable Vāmanārya.

The Jyotiṣṭoma is prepared [as follows]: in the world of Vārkajaṃbha, the Dairghaśravasa for Gaurīvita; the Bārhaduktha for Śyāvāśva; the Śyaita for Udvaṃśīya; and the Nārmedha for Nṛmedha. If it is a night-sacrifice, everything else is the same as in the Sāṃvatsarika [Sattra]. In the world of Āyu Vārkajaṃbha, the Maidhātitha for Gaurīvita; the Raurava for Śyāvāśva; the Naudhasa for Udvaṃśīya; and the Nārmedha for Nṛmedha. If it is a night-sacrifice, everything else is the same as in the Sāṃvatsarika [Sattra]. In the world of Āyu Vārkajaṃbha, the Maidhātitha for Gaurīvita; the Raurava for Śyāvāśva; the Naudhasa for Udvaṃśīya; and the Nārmedha for Nṛmedha. If it is a night-sacrifice, everything else is the same as in the Sāṃvatsarika [Sattra].

"Abhi pra gopatim gira" is the *ājya* for the *abhijit* [day] of the Brahman; if it is an *atirātra*, the *śyāvāśva*, *pramam̐hiṣṭhīya*, *hārivarṇa*, and *nārmedha* [stotras] are in the place of the *sāmatṛca*; "pratyasmai pipīṣata" is the *nānada*, the *ṣoḍaśin-sāman*; the night is the *saṃdhi*; the rest is the same as in the *sāṃvatsarika* [rite]. 314.

3.4 "Pavasvendram accha" is the *satrāsāhīya*, *śrudhya*, and *saphaśrudhya* [stotras]; if it is an *atirātra*, the *āndhīgava* is in the place of the *sāmatṛca*; the *jyotiṣṭoma-atirātra* with the *ṣoḍaśin* at the end; the rest is the same as in the *sāṃvatsarika*. 315. 3.5
"Vratasyā no viśvāsu havyam"—this is the Śyaita Brahman-sāman; the Audala belongs to the world of Gaurīvita; the rest is the same as in the [ritual] lasting a year. 316. 3.6.

"Flow on as the leader of speech, with flashing luster"—this is the *rāthaṃtara*. "O Sage Agni, come to the feast"—these three [verses] belong to the *bārhata* [meter]. "According to his ancient splendor"—this is the *gāyatra* and the *cāmahīyava*. "Pour out the pressed juice on every side"—this is the *samanta*, the *rāthaṃtara*, the *dairghaśravasa*, and the *yaudhājaya*. "This Soma"—the last [verse] is the *pārtha*; [then follow] the *bṛhat* and the *vāmadevya*. "From the sweet [juice], thus, from the center"—this is the *śyaita*; [then follows] the *kāleya* among its own [verses].

With the verses "svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā" (the Gāyatra-saṃhita), "pavasvendram accha" (the Saphaśrudhya), and "purojitī vo andhasaḥ" (the Śyāvāśva-andhīgava); with verses containing the word "sūrya," the last [laud] is the Kāva; the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Yajñāyajñīya. The Bahiṣpavamāna is Trivṛt; the Ājya-lauds are Trivṛt; the Mādhyandina-pavamāna is Saptadaśa; the Pṛṣṭha of the Hotṛ is Pañcadaśa; that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is Pañcadaśa; that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is Pañcaviṃśa; that of the Acchāvāka is Saptadaśa; the Ārbhava is Ekaviṃśa; and the Agniṣṭoma is Ekaviṃśa. 32.3.7.

"Let us choose Agni as the messenger"—with this [verse], both types of *ājya* chants are performed; the *Śrāyantīya* is the *brahmasāman*; "That exhilaration of yours which is most excellent" is the *gāyatra* [sāman] on the *aukṣa* verses; the *āndhīgava*, the *sākamaśva*, the *saubhara*, the *traikakubha*, and the *vaidhaśīya* follow after [the *āndhīgava*]; these are the *uktha* chants. The *ārbhava* [pavamāna] is the twenty-four-fold; the *agniṣṭoma* is the twenty-one-fold; it is accompanied by the *ukthas*. The rest is the same as the previous [rite], with the same *stomas*. 332 3.9

"Sing forth to him, O men; sing well to him who is born, the overcomer of waters. Flow on as the foremost of speech, with a flashing luster! O Sage Agni, come hither for the feast of Pavamāna. Even from afar, the singers sing loudly to Indra; great is the homage to Indra and Agni. High is your birth from the pressed juice. Thus [is] the Gāyatra and the Āmahīyava. "Flow on, most rich in honey"—this is the *saṃkṣāra* of the *iḍās*. "The ancient, primordial, praiseworthy nectar"—this is the Yaudhājaya for three verses. "O Soma, being purified... [etc.]

One should maintain the *raurava* on one verse, the *rathantara* on three verses, and the *vāmadevya* with the verse "The child being born, the beloved, they cleanse him. The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra]; the *svāra-sāman* is based on the verses of the *vāmadevya*; the *sauparṇa*, the *śrāyantīya*, and the *kāleya* are used; the *gāyatra-saṃhita* is used with the verse "With the sweetest, most intoxicating [Soma]"; the *sapha* and *śrudhya* are used with the verse "Run forth toward Indra"; the *śyāvāśva* and *āndhīgava* are used with the verses beginning "For you, through the conquest of the soma-juice"; the *kāva* is used with the verses concerning the Sun; and the *yajñāyajñīya* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.

The *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold (*trivṛt*); the three *ājya* stotras are fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*); the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s [stotra] is threefold; the midday *pavamāna* is seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*), as is the *hotṛ*’s *pṛṣṭha*; the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s [stotra] is fifteenfold; the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s is twenty-fivefold (*pañcaviṃśa*); the *acchāvāka*’s is seventeenfold; the *ārbhava* is seventeenfold; and the *agniṣṭoma* is twenty-onefold (*ekaviṃśa*). 34.3.10.

"Sing forth to him, O men! Pavamāna has brought [the light] forth. "Of thee, the purifying one, who indeed? "Hither, even now, we call upon you as our friend. "For I have obtained this thought from my father, a beautiful [song]. "High up is thy birth from the pressed juice"—with these verses, the *gāyatra* [sāman] is on one verse; the *āmahīyava* on one; the *śākvaravarṇa* on one; "Being purified, O Soma, in thy stream"—the *vaiṣṭambha* on one; the *kāleya* on one; the *yaudhājaya* on one; and the *auśana* as the final [verse]; then the *rathantara* and the *vāmadevya*.

The *saubhara* is on the verses of the *śrāyantīya*; the *vāravantīya* is on the verses of the *kāleya*; the *gāyatra* and the *svāśira* are on the verse "svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā"; the *arka* is on the verse "pavasva indram accha"; the *sapha*, *āsyeya*, *purojitī vaḥ andhasaḥ*, the *śyāvāśva*, the *āndhīgava*, the *kāva*, and the final *yajñāyajñīya* are the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*. This is the arrangement for the latter [rite]; its *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*), and both [the *stoma* and the *sāman*] are threefold (*trivṛt*).

Before the *śākvara* verse, there is the *svāra* [sāman]; the *sauparṇa* belongs to Āyāsya; the *pauṣkala* is in the world of [the gods]; before the *śyāvāśva*, there is the *aiḍa* belonging to Āyāsya; the two latter *pavamāna* chants of the *caturviṃśa* [stoma] are arranged in *tṛcas*; the rest is the same as the previous [rite], having the same *stoma*.

362. 3.13 The *rathaṃtara* belongs to Dairghaśravas; the *aiḍa* belonging to Āyāsya is between [the others]; after the *samhitā* on a single [verse], there is the *jarābodhīya*; the rest is the same as the one-day (*aikāhika*) *viśvajit* *agniṣṭoma*; the two latter *pavamāna* chants have eighteen verses; the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha* has twenty-one verses; the *agniṣṭoma* [finale] is twenty-one-fold; everything else is threefold (*trivṛt*). 363. 3.14

As Pavamāna strikes down [the foes], being purified, he has stepped forth. O Sage, as you are being purified, may Agni strike down the Vṛtras. I invoke Mitra, whose will is pure. May the Soma-drops exhilarate you; I invoke those two for whom this Soma flows most brilliantly. Thus, on one verse there is a *gāyatra* chant, on another a *vārṣāhara*, and on another a *śākvaravarṇa*. With "O Soma, being purified, flow in your stream," on one verse there is a *vaṣaṭkāranidhana*, on another a *raurava*, and on another a *yaudhājaya*. The final [verse] is the *auśana*; and there are the *rathantara* and the *vāmadevya*.

The *Bṛhat* and the *Kāleya*, with the verse "O most excellent one, that intoxication of yours... for the *Gāyatra*; the *Vārṣāhara*, with "Flow on, O Pavamāna, go to Indra... for the *Sapha* and *Aupagava*; the *Nānada*, with "For you, through the impulse of the soma-juice... for the *Andhīgava*; the *Kāva* as the final [laud], and the *Yajñāyajñīya* as the *Agniṣṭoma-sāman*. The *Trivṛt* *Pavamāna* lauds and the *Agniṣṭoma-sāman* [are used]; and the *Ājya* and *Pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are performed with three verses each. 37. 3.15.

"Sing forth to him, O men!"—with this one verse [they perform] the Bahiṣpavamāna. The Ājya-stotras are the Sadyaḥkrāṇa chants. "O Indu, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts"—this is the Gāyatra. "Being purified, O Soma, in your stream"—this is the Utsedha. The last [verse] is the Auśana. The Rathantara and Vāmadevya are the Niṣedha of the Śrāyantīya; its Ṛk is in its own [verses]. The Kāleya is performed with the verses beginning "With that luster, with the golden [stream], being purified. The Gāyatrastotra is the Yajñāyajñīya, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. The Stoma is the Ekatrika: [performed] with one verse, then with three, [then with three]—38. 3.16.

The *jyotiṣṭoma* [is performed with]: "O Agni, with all fires," "O Agni," "O Mitra and Varuṇa," "These [Somas]," "Sit down," "O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed juice," and "High is the birth of the plant"—this is the *gāyatra* and the *āmahīyava*. "Flow on, most honey-sweet," this is the *kāleya*; "O Soma, for you first the grass was strewn," this is the *yaudhājaya*; "Being purified, O Soma, with your stream," this is the *raurava* and the *auśana*, the last being the *rathantara* and the *vāmadevya*; and "Now indeed, O Indra, lover of songs," and "Pour the drop for Indra."

The *dyautāna* belongs to the Maruts; "with the sweetest, with the most intoxicating" is the *gāyatra-saṃhitā*; "run forth like a roaring [horse] of the flowing waters" is the *sapha-śrudhya*; "come forward" is the *marut-saṃstobha*; "for you, with the conquest of the soma-juice" is the *śyāvāśva-andhīgava*; the final hymn of the *kava* is "the god who bestows wealth upon you"; the *yajñāyajñīya* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*; the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the three *ājya* stotras are the *pañcadaśa*; the *ṣoḍaśin* belongs to the *acchāvāka*; the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* is the *ṣoḍaśa*; and the [other stotras] are the *saptadaśa*.

There are three *pṛṣṭha* stotras; the *ṣoḍaśin* belongs to the *acchāvāka*; the *ārbhava* is the *ṣoḍaśa*; and the *agniṣṭoma* is the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*). (39) 3.17 "Eté asṛgram indavo yavaṃ-yavaṃ no andhasā"—with this [verse] as the *purastātparyāsa*, there are two triplets or two tetrads for the *āyuṣa* hymns, the *ṣoḍaśa* *pavamāna*s, and the *acchāvāka*sāmans; the *agniṣṭoma* is the twenty-one-fold. There are two *uktha*s, and the rest is the same as the previous [rite], having the same *stoma*. (3101) 3.18

"O Indu, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts"—this is the Gāyatra; "and the Amahīyava"; "Flow on, most honey-sweet"—this is the Kāleya; "Thee, O Soma, the first ones who have spread the sacrificial grass"—this is the Dairghaśravasa; "Being purified, O Soma, in thy stream"—these are the Raurava and Yaudhājaya; "In the world of Śrudhi, of the Maruts"—this is the *saṃstobha* of the Maruts; "The *saṃstobha* of the Maruts"—this is the Śyāvāśva; "For you, with the impulse of the juice"—this is the Āndhīgava. The two subsequent Pavamānas consist of the Trivṛt stoma; the rest is the same as the first Vrātyastoma. 3102 3.19.

The *pratipad* for the first [pressing] is the *agriyavatī*; the morning pressing consists of the *gāyatra* "uccā te jātam andhasaḥ" and the *āmahīyava*; the *kāleya* "pavasva madhumattamaḥ"; the *dairghaśravasa* "tve soma prathamā vṛktabarhiṣaḥ"; the *rathaṃtara* "punānaḥ soma dhārayā"; the *raurava* and *yaudhājaya*; the *pārtha* "vṛṣā śoṇaḥ," which is the final [stotra]; the *bṛhat* and the *vāmadevya*; and the *dyautāna* "adhā hīndra gīrvaṇaḥ" and "indum indrāya śiñcata," with the *svādiṣṭhayā*.

With "madiṣṭhayā" [is] the Gāyatra-saṃhitā; the Jarābodhīya and the Svāśira [are] the Ārka; with "pari pra dhanva" and "nadaṃ va odatīnām" [is] the Saphaśrudhya; with "pary ū ṣu" [is] the Marut-saṃstobha; with "purojitī vo andhasaḥ" [are] the Śyāvāśva and Andhīgava; the Ātharvaṇa and the Bṛhat are for Agni; the Kāva is the final [part]; "devo vo draviṇodāḥ" [is] the Yajñāyajñīya, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman; there are two Trivṛt stotras, two Pañcadaśa and Saptadaśa, and two Ekaviṃśa and Caturviṃśa.
Forty-four, forty-eight, two thirty-nines, two thirty-threes, and two thirty-twos: 311. 3.20.

"O Agni, you purify our lifespans; O Agni, the purifier, with your radiance; Agni is the head of heaven, the summit; O Agni, come for the feast; who among men is your kinsman, worthy of praise and homage? May Agni strike down the Vṛtras; great are the flames he has given"—with these verses, one [verse] is in the *gāyatrī* meter, one is the *āmahīyava*, one is the *jarābodhīya*, and "Protect us, O Agni" is one [verse]; the *yaudhājaya* is on three [verses], "O King, the messenger, well-kindled" is the *auśana*, and "With this homage to your Agni" and "Which of yours, O Agni, O Aṅgiras? is the *rathantara*.

The *Vāmadevya*, "O Agni, come with the fires," and "Toward us, O you of sharp brilliance"—these are the *Naudhasa* and *Kāleya*; "Unassailable one, go forward"—these are the *Gāyatra-saṃhita*; "Auspicious is our Agni when invoked," and "O Agni, of booty consisting of cattle"—these are the *Sapha* and *Pauṣkala*; "You, the guest of every people"—this is the *Śyāvāśva-āndhīgava*; "The kindled Agni with fuel, with song I praise"—this is the *Yajñāyajñīya*; "The sisters approach thee"—this is the *Vāravantīya*, the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* among the *Vāyavyā* verses. 312. 3.21.

This is the arrangement for the Uttara[-sāman]: its Agniṣṭomasāman is the Vāravantīya upon the Revatī verses; both [the Bahiṣpavamāna and the Agniṣṭomasāman] are Trivṛt. He extracts the Jarābodhīya from before the Yaudhājaya; the Raurava is in the place of the Pauṣkala; the Śrudhya belongs to Śyāvāśva; the Yajñāyajñīya is [extracted] from the Yajñāyajñīya; the Kāva [is extracted] from the Yajñāyajñīya. The rest is the same as the previous Jyotiṣṭoma Stoma.

"Protect us with your aids, O Agni; let our prayers impel Agni"—with these two verses, consisting of three and five *ṛc*s respectively, as the *paryāsa* (concluding verse), he recites "Protect us, O Agni, with one [aid]" (*pāhi no agna ekayā*) in the *raurava* melody over three verses, the *dairghaśravasa* over one verse, the *samanta* in the *viṣṭārapaṅkti* meter, and the *yaudhājaya* over three verses.
The rest is the same as before; the entire chant consists of seventeen verses. 3.24.3133.24.

"Flow on, O Indu, as the pressed bull!"—these drops have been released. "O Sage, of you who are being purified, these are the Vratya-offerings and the butter-oblations; high is the birth of your juice"—thus [the verses]. On one [verse] is the Gāyatra; on one, the Āmahīyava; on one, the Jarābodhīya. "Being purified, O Soma, in your stream"—on three [verses] in their own [tunes], the Naudhasa hymns; the Abhīvarta is the Brahman-sāman; the rest is the same as in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
This indeed is the midday pressing of the subsequent [sacrifice]; the rest is entirely like the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In the world of the Śākvara-stotra, the *jarabodhīya* is the *vaṣaṭkāranidhana* of the Saptaha; the *vaṣaṭkāranidhana* of the Bṛhat is the same as that of the Śyena; the rest is identical. 3136 3.27

The Soma juices have flowed forth; resounding like chariots, the drops have sped along their paths, filling out the sacrifice. Sing forth to Mitra, sing forth the gladdening song to Indra; the chanters of hymns sing it forth for you both, as do the wise Soma-drops. "Pra somā devavītaye" is the Gāyatra; "Pra tu drava" is the Auśana; the final [verse] is the Vāmadevya, the Maidhātitha, the Hārāyaṇa, and the Kaulmalabarhiṣa; and "Pra somāso madacyuta" is the Gāyatra.

*abhi dyumnaṃ bṛhadyaśaḥ pra dhanva soma jāgṛviḥ* (for the Bhārgava); *pra sunvānāyāndhasaḥ satrāsāhīye* (for Śyāvāśva Audala); *pro ayāsīt* is the final [verse] of the Kava; *pra daivodāso agniḥ* is the *Agniṣṭomasāman* called the *Yajñāyajñīya*, belonging to Dairghaśravasa, [to be sung] in its own [verses]. If he should live, [the chant] is entirely *svāra*; all [stotras] are *trivṛt*. The *Vāmadevya* is peace; the *Vāmadevya* is peace. 314. 3.28. The Third Chapter on the Vivṛti.

Now, regarding those one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) which were prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa by means of the four chapters beginning with the sixteenth, their ritual arrangement (*klṛpti*) is here stated by means of three [chapters].

The Jyotiṣṭoma—its time of commencement, initiation (*dīkṣā*), the days of the *upasad* rites, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth—is described in the Sūtra by four chapters beginning with "the northern course of the sun" (*udagayana*) and "the first fortnight" (*pūrvapakṣa*). Among those, we shall here explain the procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the Udgātṛ priest, and not anything else; for that has been explained by Āpastamba and others as being dependent upon the Adhvaryu. In this regard, he states the ritual arrangement (*klṛpti*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma as declared in the section beginning, "Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning":
"The Jyotiṣṭoma is arranged. (1)

"Prajāpati desired, 'May I become many, may I procreate. He saw this Agniṣṭoma," and so forth; the meaning is that the Jyotiṣṭoma, having the Agniṣṭoma as its concluding form (saṃsthā), is established by the Brāhmaṇa. In the section on the one-day sacrifices (ekāha), the Brāhmaṇa first prescribes its concluding form and its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). As it has been said: "The restatement is for the purpose of prescribing the remaining details. Its performance has already been shown by us [previously]. || 1 ||
Thus ends the Jyotiṣṭoma. || 1 ||
Now, this cow has been described by the section beginning with "gaur ity eṣa gauḥ. He states its ritual application:
The cow. || 1 ||

In the world of Vārkajaṃbha, [one sings] the Dairghaśravasa; for Dairghaśravasa, the Bārhaduktha; for his own [world], the Śyaita; for Gaurīvita, the Śyāvāśva; for Udvaṃśīya, the Nārmedha—if it be night. || 2 ||
The rest is the same as that for the annual [Soma sacrifice]. || 3 ||

Thus [it is said]. The *gauḥ* (the "Cow") is established in the *Gavāmayana* by the penultimate section of the second chapter. In that context, regarding the sixth day of the repeated *abhiplava* period, which is a *rāthaṃtara*, it is stated that there would be a state of redundancy (*jāmitā*) upon its conjunction with the *rāthaṃtara-āyus* [sāman]; therefore, to avoid that, the *vārkajaṃbha* *bṛhat*-finale (*nidhana*) was prescribed for the *āyus* at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*). For it is said in the *Nidāna-sūtra*: "Now, where there is a conjunction at the end of a common *sāman*, they call that a state of redundancy; or where there are two days with a common *pṛṣṭha*."

In this regard, there are these eight causes of *jāmi* (redundancy): the *saubhara*, the verses containing the word "ancient" (*pratnavatyaḥ*), the *bṛhat* [sāman], this utterance (*abhivyāhāraḥ*), the *vārka-jambha* with the *bṛhat* finale, the statement "the *bṛhat*-finale ones," and the phrase "in the cases of the *rathantara* conjunctions. However, the *vārka-jambha* has the *ī* finale. This is so that there may not be a separation between two *sāmans*. The *go* [sāman], which accompanies the *āyus*, is performed at the midday pressing.

Since the life-span [of the sacrifice] is limited to a single day (*aikāhika*), and because of the absence of *jāmi* (redundancy), one will extract the *bṛhannidhana* for the *vārkajaṃbha*. Thus, in the *goṣṭoma*, having extracted its accompanying *īnidhana* as well, the *dairghaśravasa* should always be performed in its place. And for the sake of non-confusion, the *bārhaduktha* belongs to that. Because the *indrakratu* is employed in the second fortnight of the *gavāmayana*, here the *svāsuśyaita* is used. Since the *gaurīvit* is employed in a sacrificial session (*satra*), in its place the original *śyāvāśva* alone is used.

If the Goṣṭoma should be concluded with an Atirātra, then for the Udvamśīya there are Nārmedha verses in various meters; this is because it is heard that these are the form of day and night, as they possess the character of the night. All else is the same as in the Gavāmayana sacrifice by means of the Gava-stotra. Its arrangement is as follows: *pavasva vāco agriyo davidyutatyā rucā*, *pavasvendo vṛṣā sutaḥ*, *vṛṣā soma dyumānasi*, and *pavamānasya te kave*—this is the Bahiṣpavamāna.

*agnindumitram*, *vayamindramidgāḥ*—these four verses [are for Indra]. *indre agniḥ* [is the first] *ājya*. *asya pratnām* [is] the *gāyatra* and the *cāmahīyava*. *parītoṣi* [is used] throughout the first [verse]. *Dairghaśravasa* and *bārhaduktha* [are used] in the three [verses]. *Yaudhājaya* [is used] in the middle verse. *Ayaṃ somaḥ* [is] the final *pārtha*—thus [is] the midday [service]. *Bṛhat*, *vāmadevya*, *śyaita*, and *kāleya* are the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. *yaste mado vareṇyaḥ* [is] the *gāyatra* in the *aukṣa* [laud].

"Pavasva indram accha" is for Sapha Śrudhi; "Purojitī vo andhasaḥ" is for Śyāvaśva Andhīgava. The Ārbhava [Stotra] consists of verses containing the word "sūryavatī," with the last being the Kāva. The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Yajñāyajñīya. The Ukthas consist of the Sākamaśva, Saubhara, and Udvaṃśīya; however, in the Atirātra configuration, the Nārmedha is the last of the Ukthas. The Bahiṣpavamāna has the fifteen-fold (pañcadaśa) Stoma. The Ājya-stotras have the nine-fold (trivṛt) Stoma. The midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina savana) has the seventeen-fold (saptadaśa) Stoma. The third pressing has the twenty-one-fold (ekaviṃśa) Stoma. It includes the Ukthas.
The night [stotras] have the fifteen-fold Stoma, and the junction (saṃdhi) has the nine-fold Stoma—such is the arrangement of the Stomas.
Life:
Now, this life has been described by the Anuvāka beginning with "This is life" (āyur etad).
[This is] of life. || 1 ||

In the world of Vārkajaṃbha, [one sings] the *maidhātitha*; in that of Maidhātithi, the *raurava*; in his own [world], the *naudhasa*; in that of Gaurīvīta, the *śyāvāśva*; in that of Udvaṃśīya, the *nārmedha*—if it is night.
The rest is the same as that for the annual [sacrifice]. || 3 ||

Thus: in the *Gavāmayana*, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is established as the *Āyuḥ-kalpa* by means of the section beginning with "The *Ājya* and *Bahiṣpavamāna*. Regarding its one-day (*ekāha*) form, the modification of the substances has been stated. The *Nidāna* is easy to understand according to what precedes it. The *Bahiṣpavamāna* consists of [the verses] beginning with "upāsmai" and "vipaścit. The *Ājya* stotras consist of "agna ā yāhi," "no mitro," and "indrāgnī. The *Gāyatra* and *Cāmahīyava* are [performed] with the verse "uccā te"; the first [verse] has two *hiṃkāras*. The *Maidhātitha* is performed on three [verses]; the *Raurava* on three [verses]; the *Yaudhājaya* on the middle [verse]; and the *Auśana* is the final [verse].
The Rathantara, Vāmadevya, Naudhasa, and Kāleya are the Pṛṣṭha chants.

The *gāyatra-saṃhitā* verses are "svādiṣṭhayā" and so forth; the *sapha-pauṣkala* verses are "pavasvendram accha" and so forth; the *śyāvāśva-andhīgava* verses are "purojitī" and so forth; and the last [verse] belongs to Kava.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.

The *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya*, the *hārivarṇa*, and the *udvaṃśīya* are the *uktha* hymns. The *kakubh* is the meter of the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya*; the *uṣṇih* is the meter of the *hārivarṇa*. If it is an *atirātra* sacrifice, then the *nārmedha* takes the place of the *udvaṃśīya*.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is threefold; the *ājya* chants are fifteenfold.

The midday pressing consists of seventeen [stomas]; the third pressing consists of twenty-one. It includes the *uktha* chants; the night consists of fifteen [stomas]; and the *sandhi* (junction) consists of nine—such is the *stoma*. The designation "Trikadruka" refers to the aforementioned triad of *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*, according to the scriptural statement: "These indeed are the Trikadruka *stomas*. (3)
Thus [ends the section on] life-span. 3.

The Abhijit sacrifice, as well as the Abhijit and Viśvajit sacrifices, are mentioned in the Anuvāka beginning with "Prajāpati created offspring. The Viśvajit is also treated in the two subsequent Anuvākas. Therein, he explains the ritual arrangement (*klṛpti*) of the Abhijit.
